fonte: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
titulo: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
resumo: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query.This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories.We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation.To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a statetransition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, modelensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts.Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answeronly evaluation.The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/ FinHopper/.

fonte: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
titulo: Sealed Before the Open: A Verifiable Standard for Measuring AI Forecasts of Financial Markets
resumo: Related: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels, accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? Version of record: SSRN 7653679, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7653679. Cite that version. The same text is also at polyhelper.ai/research/sealed-before-the-open/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/sealed-before-the-open. The registered predictions of Section 8 are on OSF: 10.17605/OSF.IO/9Q86N. The immutable release of the open league files on which every number of the paper rests: 10.5281/zenodo.23552700. The live league and its open data (CC BY 4.0): trends.polyhelper.ai/markets, trends.polyhelper.ai/api/v1. This deposit is an archival copy made so that the full text stays retrievable; it makes no separate claim. When an AI model says gold will rise, a reader can score the call at the close but usually cannot check when it was made. A backtest mixes memory with skill, and a trading season is one path through the market. I propose a standard of numbered requirements for measuring AI forecasts of financial markets and document its reference implementation, the open league AI Council · Markets, run by PolyHelper, with a published status per requirement. Fourteen large language models, seven from US and seven from Chinese laboratories, answer the same question on a shared price snapshot, each with its own account. Eleven of them forecast twelve indicators at four horizons before each New York open. Each counted answer is sealed into a SHA-256 hash chain before its reference price and anchored in Bitcoin through OpenTimestamps. From 21 October 2026 the counted run is declared in advance, and independent RFC 3161 authorities sign every stamped record, which also enters the Sigstore Rekor transparency log. On that first counted morning every counted answer was signed before the 09:30 ET open, eight of them 29 minutes before it. The Brier score of the event asked is set against a 50% benchmark, the climatological base rate and prediction-market prices, and agreement is reported as a count of independent voices. On the development mornings of 19 and 20 October the models' probability pictures were as alike as those of about 1.6 independent forecasters. On 20 October three of the four closest pairs joined a US and a Chinese laboratory. Against a dated map of 23 AI forecasting and trading efforts, the league is the first live AI league on financial indicators to combine these elements. It is also the first AI market arena where seven US and seven Chinese models trade under one protocol beside readers assigned once, at random, to forecast before or after seeing the models. Thirty dated predictions, registered on OSF before posting, are scored in dated revisions.

titulo: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?
resumo: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.

titulo: Cogito: A Cognitive Agentic Framework Driven by Dynamic Graph of Thoughts for Financial Report Generation
resumo: Financial report generation is a complex task that requires gathering and reasoning over multi-source information. Recent advances in Large Language Models have made them a promising solution for automating this process. However, the reasoning paths in traditional Chain-of-Thought paradigms are inherently constrained by predefined, static computational topologies, rendering them ill-equipped to handle the dynamic uncertainties of real-world financial environments. To tackle this challenge, we propose Cogito, a cognitively grounded agentic framework for professional financial report generation. At its core, Cogito is driven by Dynamic Graph of Thoughts, a novel reasoning mechanism that models the agent's reasoning process as an evolving topology for adaptive exploration.We further introduce a Social Collaboration Mechanism to facilitate coordinated agent interaction. Finally, Cogito is instantiated as a multi-agent system, where four specialized agents collaboratively execute the end-to-end report generation task. Extensive experiments on enterprise- and industry-level financial report generation benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of Cogito in data quality, analytical validity, and presentation quality.

titulo: The Zytra AI Risk Atlas: A Structured Taxonomy of 141 Risks for Agentic and Foundation-Model AI Deployment in Banking and Financial Services Methodology, Coverage Architecture, Deployment-Pattern Tagging, and Benchmark Validation Against Peer Frameworks
FinDriftBench: A Synthetic Benchmark Dataset for Freshness-Aware Agentic Financial Decision Support
resumo: This dataset supports the manuscript \u201cFinDriftBench: A Freshness-Aware Benchmark for Agentic Financial Decision Support.\u201d It contains a synthetic benchmark package for evaluating agentic large language model systems under financial information drift. The dataset includes versioned financial artifacts, benchmark tasks, ground-truth labels, system configuration files, deterministic evaluation outputs, and reproducibility documentation. The benchmark covers seven task families: regulatory updates, corporate actions, market data freshness, product term updates, index methodology changes, risk-policy drift, and earnings-guidance revisions. The implemented dataset contains 105 synthetic artifacts, 70 benchmark tasks, six evaluated configurations, and 420 deterministic evaluation runs. It is designed to test whether retrieval-augmented and agentic AI systems can distinguish current authoritative evidence from stale but semantically relevant evidence. All data are synthetic and do not contain proprietary financial records, customer data, personally identifiable information, or live trading data.

titulo: GenAI-supported portfolio assessment for complex thinking: a GPT-based innovation in business education
resumo: This study examines the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into rubric-based qualitative assessment to strengthen authentic evaluation and complex thinking competencies in business education. Conducted at a graduate business school in Peru with 120 student portfolios, the research adopted a qualitative exploratory-documentary approach, complemented by a correlational analysis between human and AI evaluations to enhance the interpretive validity of the findings. A pilot subsample ( n = 12) was used for the correlational analysis comparing human and AI-assisted assessments, while descriptive analyses of complex thinking levels were conducted on the full sample ( n = 120) using the AI agent. The study employed the GPT-eComplex Assistant, a GenAI-based evaluator developed from ChatGPT and configured with the eComplex rubric, to identify recurring patterns, strengths, and areas for improvement without replacing human pedagogical judgment. The findings revealed that: (a) the GPT-eComplex Assistant closely mirrored human evaluators’ judgments, reinforcing consistency, traceability, and transparency, although still requiring teacher calibration; (b) the digital portfolio served as an authentic learning artifact to capture systemic and critical thinking, while showing limitations in the scientific dimension; (c) the use of GenAI for assessment in higher education remains incipient and under-researched, underscoring the need for empirical evidence and ethical guidelines; and (d) the responsible integration of GenAI demands active teacher mediation, ethical awareness, and institutional transparency, ensuring that technology complements rather than replaces pedagogical judgment. This study contributes a pedagogical strategy that combines formative portfolio assessment, AI-supported co-evaluation, and the AI-PROMPT Framework, offering a replicable model for embedding GenAI into authentic, reflective, and ethically grounded assessment practices in higher education. The results represent an innovative contribution by positioning GPT as a complementary tool in authentic assessment, reinforcing the central role of human judgment and opening new perspectives for AI-supported evaluation in the Ibero-American and beyond.

titulo: Bridging the Probabilistic-Deterministic Divide: A Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Verifiable Regulatory Compliance in Generative Financial Agents
resumo: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into the financial services sector has precipitated a paradigm shift in customer engagement, algorithmic trading, and automated advisory services. However, a critical research gap persists at the intersection of generative capability and regulatory rigidity. While LLMs exhibit unprecedented fluency and semantic understanding, they fundamentally operate as probabilistic engines, making them inherently ill-suited for the deterministic requirements of financial compliance frameworks such as the European Union’s Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II), the EU AI Act, and the United States Securities and Exchange Commission’s Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI). This research paper identifies and addresses the "Reasoning Gap" in current Conversational AI literature the inability of pure Transformer-based architectures to guarantee logically sound, verifiable, and legally compliant financial advice without hallucination. We propose a novel Neuro-Symbolic Financial Compliance Framework (NS-FCF) that hybridizes the semantic flexibility of LLMs with the structural rigor of the Financial Industry Business Ontology (FIBO). By leveraging logic-enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Program of Thought (PoT) prompting, this framework offers a pathway toward "Verifiable Autonomous Finance," ensuring that AI-generated advice is not only human-like in interaction but mathematically and legally provable in its derivation.

fonte: Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area International Conference on Digital Economy and Artificial Intelligence (DEAI)
titulo: Research on Financial Statement Checking Relationship Recognition System Based on Large Language Models
resumo: With the driving power of the internet wave, the auditing industry faces unprecedented challenges and opportunities. Traditional audit methods increasingly reveal weaknesses at processing vast data, which requires the application of new technologies to maximize the efficiency and accuracy of audit. As an epoch-making innovation of natural language processing, Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate unequalled performance at parsing texts, semantic detection, and text generation, opening up approaches to forward-looking intelligent reform of auditing. This paper researches the innovation of LLMs to be utilized to intelligent Checking relationship detection of financial statements, to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of auditing.Based on the combination of the knowledge base of audit with the technologies of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), we introduce a multi-agent system to intelligent Checking relationship detection of financial statements. LLMs can automatically identify and certify Checking relationships between financial statements, dramatically improving audit efficiency and quality. Environmental context and data support are provided through the audit knowledge base, and the RAG technologies enhance the power of analysis. This paper demonstrates, through experiments, that these technologies can support intelligent Checking relationship detection, ushering auditing into an intelligent audit era.

titulo: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
resumo: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).

titulo: Governing the Machine: A Reference Architecture for Trustworthy Agentic AI in Enterprise Finance and Supply Chain
Who Keeps the Gains from Personal AI Assistants? Seller Adaptation and the Unassisted in a Language-Model Market Simulation
resumo: Personal AI assistants are beginning to transact for consumers, and early adopters capture real savings. Whether those savings survive, and what happens to consumers who have no assistant, depends on how sellers respond -- a question single-user evidence cannot answer. We build an agent-based rental market in which language models play consumers, assistants, and six adaptive sellers guided by an algorithmic pricing tool. Half the population receives an assistant under an advisory or an executing mandate; the contract pairs a fee only the renter's physical action avoids with a pre-selected add-on an authorised assistant can cancel online. An analytical benchmark and a behaviourally calibrated rule market supply ex-ante predictions, and paired branches with frozen versus adaptive sellers separate adoption effects from market feedback. Across thirty simulated markets, executing assistants cut adopters' spending by 13.7 USD per renter-day when sellers are frozen; adaptation claws back about a third, leaving 8.7, with the gains arriving both as lower bills and as rentals completed at all. Sellers raise headline rates while cutting fees, and the calibrated forecast of the burden on unassisted consumers (+3.6) does not transfer: their mean spending change is +0.4, confidence interval -0.6 to +1.3. Seller-model swaps and a within-market transfer of fee-setting to the pricing tool show that fee conduct, and with it the division of the gains, is decided on the seller side. Assistants, we conclude, should be evaluated at market level -- completion, total spending, and non-users included -- and the comparison layers locate exactly where a calibrated behavioural forecast fails in a language-model market.

fonte: International Conference on Advancements in Smart, Secure and Intelligent Computing (ASSIC)
titulo: Designing an Agentic AI Prototype for Corporate Financial Optimization Using Design Science Research
resumo: Internal corporate finance has turned much more complicated, one of the reasons is liquidity uncertainty, another is market volatility and also due to the increasing length of the demand chain for financial dynamically decision-making. Unfortunately, a lot of financial systems out there still mainly focus on processing and reporting transactions, and they are not really designed for financial optimizations through intelligence. Therefore, it is a common scene that organizations suffer from inefficient liquidity allocation and idle cash resources that are really not being utilized. By employing the DSR methodology as a research method, this paper presents an Agentic AI-enabled sample of financial optimization. The suggested platform is a harmonious combination of mechanical thinking, financial analysis-related, decision for a change, a step of the investment, and decision-making under the risk of support joined in one intelligent financial advisory platform. The structure is composed of four principal levels: Input Layer, Knowledge Layer, Agentic AI Engine, and Output Layer. The Agentic AI Engine is a composite of various autonomous agents like Context Analysis Agent, Reasoning Agent, Risk Analysis Agent, and Recommendation Agent. At the core of these agents are LLM-based reasoning and RAG mechanisms that equip them with contextual comprehension and the ability to make and explain financial recommendations. Among the features implemented in the prototype are tracking of liquidity status, pinpointing opportunities for the utilization of idle cash, making an assessment of investment alternatives, and a capability of recommendation that is adaptive and is highly consistent with organizational goals and risk appetite.
